newsitem.title: USA: Maine court cannot judge bishop's negligence.
newsitem.headline: Maine court cannot judge bishop's negligence.

text.p: The Maine Supreme Court ruled on Friday in a case involving a Roman Catholic priest accused of sexual misconduct that courts did not have the right to interfere in church affairs.
The court was asked to determine if a Roman Catholic bishop was negligent in supervising a priest accused of having an affair with the wife of a churchmember.

In a four-to-two ruling, the justices said that allowing the state to decide the extent of a bishop's managerial authority would violate the church's right to practice religion without government interference.

"When a civil court undertakes to compare the relationship between a religious institution and its clergy with the agency relationship of the business world ... the risk of constitutional violation is evident," Chief Justice Daniel Wathen wrote.
The ruling blocks Albert Swanson and his wife Ruth from suing Bishop Joseph Gerry, who as head of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Portland oversees Catholic churches for all of Maine.

The Swansons sued Gerry for his alleged negligence in the supervision and training of Maurice Morin, a priest in Grey, Maine, who allegedly had an affair with Ruth Swanson after the couple had gone to him for counselling in 1990.
The incident nearly caused the Swansons to obtain a divorce, and the couple's son committed suicide because of the family's impending breakup, according to court documents.
The Swansons' suit against Morin is still pending.
In a dissenting opinion, Justic Kermit Lipez said the Supreme Court acted prematurely, and letting the trial go forward would allow the church's rights to be balanced against the Swansons' rights.

"The plaintiff's claim that the negligence of the church caused them extreme emotional distress and psychological damage emphasises that we are not dealing solely with matters of religious belief or internal church policy," Lipez wrote.
